hero.title: Automated GC-MS Data Analysis Across Instrument Formats
hero.intro: Upload one sample's GC-MS peak table and a standard file (target list). The page detects the table format, unifies compound names and CAS numbers, handles duplicate peaks and peaks with several library hits by fixed rules, finds the relative content of each target, then uses odor thresholds to compute OAV or ROAV, rank the key flavor compounds and draw a flavor profile.
scope.text: This site is designed for quick processing of a single sample: upload one file at a time, containing the peak table of one sample. To process hundreds or thousands of samples in batch, email

privacy.lead: Your data never leaves your computer.
privacy.text: Everything runs in your browser and files are never uploaded to any server. The page has no analytics or tracking, so it suits a first look at confidential company data.
privacy.v1: Method 1: once the page has loaded, disconnect from the network (turn off Wi-Fi or unplug the cable), then upload and analyze a file. Everything still works.
privacy.v2: Method 2: press F12 to open the developer tools, go to the Network panel, then upload and analyze a file. No data requests appear.
privacy.tech: The page's Content-Security-Policy only allows connections to this site; the browser blocks requests to anywhere else. Templates and settings you save stay in your own browser.
privacy.mini: Read in your browser only, never uploaded

about.peak_required: The peak table needs three columns: (1) compound name or CAS number; (2) retention time; (3) peak area or relative content (%). If the sample was quantified, add a concentration column; it is used when OAV is chosen. Retention index, match score and peak number columns are optional. Columns are recognized from header keywords or instrument templates, and you can correct them in the step "Check the header and columns".

result.summary: {n} targets in the standard file: {found} found ({manual} assigned by you), {miss} not found. Retention time range ± {win} min.
result.rel_column: Relative content is taken as it is from the peak table's relative content column (the basis option has no effect); for peaks added by rule 1 the values are added.

rel.basis_help: Without a relative content column in the peak table, the denominator is either the sum of all peak areas or the sum of the found targets' peak areas. With such a column the file's values are used as they are and this option has no effect.

log.title: Processing log
log.peak_to_closer_target: The peak at {rt} min fits both "{target}" and "{kept}"; it goes to "{kept}", whose reference retention time is closer, and "{target}" does not use it.
log.hit_chosen: The library gave several candidates for the peak at {rt} min ({hits}); the standard file decides for "{target}".
log.summed: {target}: the peaks at {rts} min within the retention time range are all identified as this compound with no peak of another compound between them; added (retention time of the largest peak, {rt} min).
log.separated: {target}: the peaks at {rts} min in the range are also identified as this compound but are separated from the peaks used by a peak of another compound; not added, possibly a misidentification.
log.elsewhere: {target}: a peak identified as this compound also appears at {rts} min, outside the retention time range; not added, possibly a misidentification.
log.no_rt_center: {target}: no reference retention time in the standard file; the range is centred on the compound's largest peak ({rt} min).
footer.examples: Example data: compound sets and concentrations from Wang et al., Food Chem X 2025 (yogurt, CC BY-NC); Xu et al., Food Chem X 2026 (pasteurized milk, CC BY-NC); Duensing et al., J Agric Food Chem 2024 (Gouda, CC BY). Everything else is simulated. Example 4 (human milk HM_Test) is an original instrument report from Cui et al., Food Bioscience 2026 (doi:10.1016/j.fbio.2026.110162); only the computer paths and the method file name were removed, and the sample name was changed to HM_Test. Its standard file holds the 75 compounds and retention times of Table S1 of that paper; 2,4-di-tert-butylphenol, 2-ethyl-1-hexanol, 2-phenoxyethanol and isophorone are migrants from sampling materials (Table S1, footnote A).

fl.title: Flavor interpretation
fl.intro: Only the targets found above are used. With quantified amounts (an amount column) the page computes OAV = amount / threshold; OAV >= 1 means the compound can be smelled in the sample. With only peak areas or relative contents it computes ROAV: the compound with the largest contribution is 100, the others are scaled by their content / threshold ratio to it. ROAV only shows relative contributions within the sample, not whether a compound can be smelled.
fl.note_oav: The peak table has an amount column, so OAV is computed; you can switch to ROAV.
fl.note_roav: The peak table has no amount column, so ROAV is computed from {basis}.
fl.basis_rel: the relative contents in the peak table
fl.unit_from_header: Unit taken from the column name "{col}"; please check.

thr.title: Odor thresholds
thr.intro: Odor thresholds of the {n} compounds found (converted to mg/kg); {miss} have none. Values from your standard file come first; where it has none, the built-in value is used (the 53 water thresholds already used by this site's Dairy Flavor Improver, cited in L.J. van Gemert (2011) Odour Thresholds, Part II). You can also change or add values here; your changes are kept in this browser only. Compounds without a threshold are not estimated and are left out.
thr.src_none: No built-in threshold, please enter one
rank.title: Key flavor compounds
rank.summary_oav: Of {n} compounds found, {key} have OAV >= 1 (can be smelled) and {mod} have OAV between 0.1 and 1; {miss} have no threshold or value and are listed at the end, not used.
rank.summary_roav: Of {n} compounds found, {key} have ROAV >= 1 (usually taken as key flavor compounds) and {mod} have ROAV between 0.1 and 1 (usually taken as modifying); {miss} have no threshold or value and are listed at the end, not used.
radar.title: Flavor profile
radar.note: Same rule as Dairy Flavor Improver: each compound's intensity I = log10({score}) (when {score} > 1, else 0) weights the GNN's odor label probabilities divided by each label's frequency in the training data (so common labels do not dominate); the {n} compounds are summed, the 12 dairy dimensions are taken and normalized, and the numbers are each dimension's share. Suited to dairy samples. The odor column above prefers knowledge-base data, but the profile needs one numeric scale, so it uses model predictions throughout.
radar.no_lift: These compounds are not in the flavor knowledge base, so they have no odor descriptors or model prediction and are not in the profile: {list}.
radar.none: No compound has an intensity above 0 and a model prediction, so there is no profile.
lim.title: Limitations
lim.1: This is a first screening based on identified compounds; it does not replace olfactometric checks such as GC-O or AEDA.
lim.2: Library search results can be misidentifications; the automatic rules (adding peaks, nearest target) only assist, and your review decides.
lim.3: Thresholds vary greatly with the medium (water, oil, milk) and between studies, often by orders of magnitude for one compound, so the results depend on the thresholds in your standard file. The built-in values are water thresholds; replace them with suitable values for other matrices.
lim.4: ROAV only shows relative contributions within the sample; OAV also ignores interactions such as synergy and masking.
lim.5: The odor labels in the profile come from this site's odor model (GNN); they are predictions, not measurements.
lim.6: Reference retention times depend on the column and method; the standard file must come from your own method.

std.required: The standard file needs three columns: (1) compound name or CAS number; (2) reference retention time; (3) odor threshold (give the unit in the column name, e.g. "Threshold (µg/kg)"). about.practice: The tool works on peak tables after integration and identification, and assumes both have been checked by hand. When processing this kind of data, adding up the peaks of the same compound takes the most time, and the most common error is several compounds in the target list matching the same peak, so one peak is counted more than once. Rule 1 (adding the peaks of the same compound within a set range centered on the reference retention time, with no peak of another compound between them) and Rule 2 (assigning a peak only to the compound with the nearest reference retention time) were written for these two problems.
about.thr_author: The built-in threshold source can be chosen on the tool page: this site's values (default, the 53 values above) or author group values. Author group values: odour detection thresholds in water taken from the L.J. van Gemert (2011) compilation and selected by the author's group for its human milk flavour research (related work: Cui et al., Food Bioscience, 2026, doi:10.1016/j.fbio.2026.110162). For compounds not in the compilation, values come from published Food Chemistry articles; each is listed with year and DOI; 2,3-octanedione is taken from Table 1 of Cui et al. (2026). Author group values are matched by CAS number (stereoisomers of one molecule can have their own values); a compound without a CAS number uses a value only when exactly one CAS number of that molecule has one. The threshold table shows the compilation page and the original study for each value.
about.thr_choice: When a threshold is uncertain, I usually check the literature on the same kind of sample; for human milk, I compare several human milk flavor studies and then choose based on my samples. With enough papers, the value is usually clear. This is why the tool asks users to enter thresholds they have checked in the standard file, and uses the built-in values only when nothing else is available.
about.thr: Odor thresholds of the compounds found are converted to mg/kg. Values from your standard file come first; where it has none, the built-in value is used (the 53 water thresholds already used by this site's Dairy Flavor Improver, cited in L.J. van Gemert (2011) Odour Thresholds, Part II). You can also change or add values on the tool page; your changes are kept in your browser only. Compounds without a threshold are not estimated and are left out.
about.radar: 12 dairy dimensions (default), the same rule as Dairy Flavor Improver: each compound's intensity I = log10(OAV or ROAV) (when it is above 1, else 0) weights the GNN's odor label probabilities divided by each label's frequency in the training data (so common labels do not dominate); the compounds are summed, the 12 dairy dimensions are taken and normalized, and the numbers are each dimension's share. Suited to dairy samples. The odor column of the ranking prefers knowledge-base data, but the profile needs one numeric scale, so it uses model predictions throughout.
about.radar_all: All 138 odor labels: each compound's intensity I = log10(OAV or ROAV) (when it is above 1, else 0) weights the GNN's probabilities for 138 odor labels (not divided by label frequency here: over 138 labels that would inflate rare labels such as cucumber a hundredfold); the compounds are summed and normalized. The chart shows the 10 largest labels as percentages of the total. Suited to non-dairy samples. The profile uses model predictions throughout.
footer.short: Everything runs in your browser. Odor labels come from this site's odor model (CC BY-NC, non-commercial academic demo only). See method & sources.
about.ident: Identification: names and CAS numbers in the peak table and the standard file are matched to the flavor knowledge base in this order: a CAS number with a valid check digit that is in the knowledge base decides, and a name pointing to another compound only gives a note (name and CAS do not agree); a CAS number that is not in the knowledge base, has a wrong check digit or was turned into a date by Excel is set aside and the name is used. Names include English and Chinese names, NIST library spellings (such as "Hexanal, 2-ethyl-") and common synonyms.
about.rel: Two ways to compute relative content (when the peak table has no relative content column; chosen under «Relative content basis» on the tool page): (1) % of all peak area (default): relative content = peak area ÷ sum of all peak areas in the table × 100, so the found targets usually add up to less than 100% and the rest are non-target peaks; (2) normalized to the targets: relative content = peak area ÷ sum of the found targets' peak areas × 100, so the targets add up to 100%. Peaks added by rule 1 count with their summed area. With a relative content column in the peak table the file's values are used as they are and the option has no effect. The total of the targets is shown below the result table. ROAV is computed from peak areas (see below); the two ways differ only by one common factor, so ROAV and the ranking do not change.
result.xlsx_hint: When a CSV is opened in Excel, CAS numbers may be turned into dates (4313-03-5 becomes 4313/3/5); use the .xlsx file instead.
about.basis_area: ROAV from peak areas is equivalent to using area-normalized relative contents, without rounding.
curve.sub: See how odor intensity depends on the concentration in air for 315 fragrance and flavor compounds, and convert a gas-phase concentration to an intensity level.
curve.gas: Concentrations are in air (gas phase); the data come from sniffing evaluations by perfumers and trained panelists.
curve.medium: Not applicable to concentrations in water, milk or other media, and not convertible from OAV or ROAV.
curve.load_failed: The curve data could not be loaded. Please check the connection and reload the page.
curve.search_label: Search by Chinese name, English name or CAS number (compare up to 4 compounds)
curve.chart_intro: Horizontal axis: log10 gas-phase concentration (µg/L air). Vertical axis: odor intensity on the LMS (0 to 100), with the intensity levels named on the right. Open circles mark the threshold (intensity 1.4, barely detectable).
curve.empty: Search for a compound and add it to draw its curve here.
curve.max: 4 compounds selected, the most that can be compared at once.
curve.full: 4 compounds are already shown. Remove one before adding another.
curve.none: Not among the 315 compounds in the source paper
curve.cas_none: Not among the 315 compounds in the source paper (CAS {cas})
curve.thr_out: Threshold {v} µg/L air, outside the plotting range of the paper
curve.step: The curve is close to a step; no conversion is given
curve.note_557_48_2: Table S2 of the Supporting Information prints the CAS number 140-88-5 (ethyl acrylate); this site uses 557-48-2, which matches the compound name.
curve.note_4166_20_5: The paper names this compound furaneol, but the CAS number given, 4166-20-5, is furaneol acetate (furaneol is 3658-77-3), so it is not known which compound was measured. Kept as published; no other page links to this curve.
curve.note_108_59_8: The paper names this compound diethyl malonate, but the CAS number given, 108-59-8, is dimethyl malonate (diethyl malonate is 105-53-3), so it is not known which compound was measured. Kept as published; no other page links to this curve.
curve.conv_label: Gas-phase concentration (µg/L air, equal to mg/m³)
curve.range: Outside the plotting range of the paper
curve.col.name: Compound
curve.src: Data: Wakayama H, Sakasai M, Yoshikawa K, Inoue M. Method for Predicting Odor Intensity of Perfumery Raw Materials Using Dose-Response Curve Database. Ind. Eng. Chem. Res. 2019, 58(32): 15036-15044, doi: 10.1021/acs.iecr.9b01225. Parameters of 314 compounds from Table S2 of the Supporting Information; isovaleric acid from Table 3 of the main text.
curve.formula: Curve: Ψ = Imax / (1 + exp(-(X - C) / D)), with X = log10(gas-phase concentration, µg/L air). The threshold is the concentration at Ψ = 1.4 (barely detectable): X = C - D · ln((Imax - 1.4) / 1.4).
curve.lms: Intensity scale: the labeled magnitude scale (LMS, 0 to 100): barely detectable 1.4, weak 6.1, moderate 17.2, strong 35.4, very strong 53.3, strongest imaginable 100.
curve.range_note: The horizontal axis runs from -5 to 5, the plotting range of the paper; outside it no value is given. For 5 compounds with D below 0.1 (such as vanillin) the curve is close to a step: they can be found, but no curve is drawn and no conversion is given.
curve.extrap: The curves are fits to the evaluation data. The paper does not give the concentration range measured for each compound; the horizontal axis from -5 to 5 is the plotting range of the paper, and parts far from the measured concentrations are extrapolation. Concentrations above the saturated vapor concentration of the compound at room temperature cannot be reached in practice, and conversions there have no meaning. For example, the saturated concentration of linalool in air at 25 °C is about 1300 µg/L (X ≈ 3).
curve.name_note: Chinese names are given for common compounds only; trade names stay in English.
curve.privacy: All calculations run in your browser; the page makes no external request.
